newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan economy seen "far from imminent crisis".
newsitem.headline: Pakistan economy seen "far from imminent crisis".

text.p: Pakistan's economy faces no immediate crisis, despite balance of payments problems and financial instability, local brokerage house Taurus Securities said in a research report received on Tuesday.
"Pakistan's current economic conditions, reflected in its performance over 1995/96 (July-June), compares favourably with trends over the past decade," the report said.
"It is far from a picture of imminent crisis."

It said the 1995/96 estimated gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate of 6.1 percent and growth in total and fixed investment at 21.8 percent and 21.5 percent respectively were significantly higher than the averages of the past 10 years.
Growth in foreign investment estimated at more than $1 billion in 1995/96 was not only 29.4 percent higher than the previous year, but 90 percent of it was long-term direct investment.
However, Taurus Securities said the external sector had continued to perform poorly. "The really weak spot is the balance of payments performance," it said.
Exports grew only 6.9 percent in dollar terms against a target of 13.6 percent, while imports rose 13.5 percent, compared to a 7.7 percent target.
Pakistan's trade deficit rose to a record $3.666 billion in 1995/96 from $2.537 billion in 1994/95. The current account deficit soared to $4.244 billion from $2.163 billion.

"In view of the last year's performance the government's targets for 1996/97 are ambitious: an increase of 16.7 percent and 3.3 percent in exports and imports to $10.04 billion and $12.06 billion respectively," Taurus Securities said.
Pakistan had a trade deficit of $443 million in October compared to $415 million in October 1995.

"Given current trends, a likely year trade deficit figure would be close to $2.8 billion," Taurus said. The current account deficit would be $3.9 billion, against government estimates of $3.1 billion, it predicted.
The report said the stock market could rise if the new caretaker government fulfilled pledges to induce fiscal discipline, curb corruption and rekindle a reform process.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, and promised to hold elections on February 3.
A caretaker cabinet led by Meraj Khalid has announced moves to cut current spending, pursue corrupt politicians and bureaucrats, and revamp the state-owned financial sector.
"The market will view these measures as largely symbolic, but necessary for the long-term growth and development of the economy and will respond positively in the next coming weeks," Taurus said.
The brokerage said foreign fund managers were still cautious about Pakistan, but a rally driven by local buying due to improved sentiment might also spark foreign trading interest.

The Karachi 100-share index fell 21.83 points, or 1.47 percent, to end at 1,464.50 on Monday, but incentives announced by the government helped the index to regain 13.96 points, or 0.95 percent, to reach 1,476.50 by noon on Tuesday.
"We expect the market to rise another 100 to 150 points from the current levels, before tapering off and settling at a higher level in the coming quarter," Taurus said.
